raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old Iranian man with renal transplant and with two tumoral lesions was admitted to our dermatology ward on March 2008. The patient was suffering from chronic renal failure due to diabetes (non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, NIDDM) for several years before this admission.
The patient developed small popular lesion (2 x 5 millimeter) on his left wrist and right leg (shin) after traveling to an endemic leishmaniasis area (Natanz in Isfahan province, Iran) in April 2006. The diagnosis of CL was confirmed by a positive direct smear for leishman bodies. As the lesions were small, they remained untreated to obtain immunity for the patient.
Due to chronic renal failure, renal transplantation was performed on the patient in August 2007. After transplantation, he received prednisolone tablets 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg daily (equivalent to 600 mg for an 80 kg patient). Several weeks after renal transplantation and immunosuppressive therapy, these small popular lesions became large cauliflower-like and tumoral lesions measured 3 x 4 x 5 cm on his left wrist and 4 x 5 x 6 cm on his right leg (shin) (Figures 1 and 2).
A slit-skin smear showed leishman bodies in Giemsa preparations. The leishmanin skin test (Montenegro) was positive with 5 mm induration.
Histopathological examination of the biopsy obtained specimens demonstrated ulcerative changes and irregular acanthosis in the epidermis, namely, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. In dermis infiltration of lymphocyte, plasma cell and histiocyte with multinucleated Giant cell were shown. Leishman bodies were seen in histiocytes, especially in the specimen obtained from the lower leg lesion (Figure 3). With regard to the clinical and histopathological findings, the diagnosis of reactivation of CL was made.
After admission to our dermatology department, he was treated with 800 mg/day IV sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam, pentavalent antimonials) for 3 weeks. In addition, his lesions were treated with local destructive cryotherapy; cryotherapy was applied by using the liquid nitrogen according to Asilian et al.. The patient responded favorably to the above treatment. Afterward, the patient was followed up for 5 years. At the latest visit on June 2013, the direct smear and polymerase chain reaction from the site of previous lesion were negative for leishman body.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male renal transplant recipient presented with two large, rapidly enlarging cauliflower-like tumoral skin lesions on his wrist and lower leg.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed small papules on his left wrist and right shin in April 2006 following travel to an endemic area, which had been intentionally left untreated. Following renal transplantation in August 2007 and initiation of high-dose immunosuppression, the quiescent lesions rapidly transformed over several weeks into massive cauliflower-like tumoral masses.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM); underwent renal transplantation in August 2007. Immunosuppressive therapy: oral prednisolone 50 mg/day and cyclosporine 7.5 mg/kg/day (600 mg daily). Prior untreated cutaneous leishmaniasis diagnosed in April 2006. Travel history: traveled to Natanz, Isfahan Province, Iran (an endemic area) in April 2006.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports rapidly enlarging exophytic masses; denies fevers, systemic pain, or graft dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 80 kg. Dermatologic examination revealed two large, exophytic, cauliflower-like tumoral lesions: one measuring 3 cm x 4 cm x 5 cm on the dorsal left wrist, and another measuring 4 cm x 5 cm x 6 cm on the right anterior lower leg (shin).
objective.advanced_workup: Cutaneous punch biopsy of leg lesion: epidermal ulceration with marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia; dermis exhibited dense infiltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes with multinucleated giant cells containing intracellular protozoa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Giemsa-stained slit-skin smear and biopsy demonstrated numerous intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman bodies) within dermal histiocytes. Leishmanin skin test (Montenegro) was reactive with 5 mm induration, confirming reactivation of cutaneous leishmaniasis induced by post-transplant immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma and deep fungal granulomas were excluded by biopsy. Management and Outcome: Treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (Pentostam) at 800 mg daily for 3 weeks, combined with serial liquid nitrogen cryotherapy sessions. The patient achieved complete clinical remission. Long-term follow-up over 5 years (through June 2013) demonstrated no recurrence, with negative repeat direct smears and negative Leishmania PCR.
